definitions.meaning: A giant slab of rock: the Earth's crust is made of many plates that sit side by side and drift.
The solid outer rock layer of the Earth, made up of giant plates.
The sinking of one plate under another where they meet: the denser plate is forced down and slides underneath.
The slow movement of the plates year after year: two plates sitting apart drift towards each other.
What happens when two moving plates push together and meet head-on.

mechanismSteps: Two giant plates of rock sit apart: the Earth's crust is made of giant slabs of rock called plates, and year after year they drift towards each other.
The plates push together: the drift becomes a push, and the two plates collide head-on where they meet.
One plate slides under the other: the denser plate is forced down and slides underneath the lighter plate - that sinking is called subduction.
Plates creep, they never lurch: a real plate moves only about two centimetres a year, slower than your fingernails grow, so the movement is a steady creep.
objectives: Name the giant slabs of rock that make up the Earth's crust
Explain what happens when two plates push together and collide
Explain what subduction means and which plate sinks
Say how fast plates really move and why the movement is a creep
subject: geography
title: Plate tectonics: giant slabs on the move

trap.explanation: A sudden jolt is easier to picture than a creep no one can feel. Plates creep, they never lurch: about two centimetres a year, slower than your fingernails grow. In the animation scene s4 the caption itself gives the warning - plates creep, they never lurch - so picture a marker creeping two centimetres in a whole year, never a sudden jump.
trap.misconception: Plates lurch in sudden jolts, snapping into new positions.

workedExample: Trace the whole chain as a worked example: start in scene s1 with the plates apart, two giant slabs of rock sitting apart and drifting towards each other year after year. In scene s2 the plates push together and collide head-on. In scene s3 the denser plate subducts, forced down to slide under the other plate - subduction is the name for that sinking. In scene s4 the speed is revealed: the movement is a creep at about two centimetres a year, slower than your fingernails grow, so the plates apart, push and collide, subduct, and creep at about 2 centimetres a year.
